course: AI Agents: What Could Go Wrong

modules.module: M1: Software That Acts, Not Just Answers

Claude.notes: Every lesson opens with a concrete real-world incident that seeds the concept, and the narrative-to-concept handoff is disciplined; the Advanced 'why does it matter' framing is present throughout and the terminal takeaways land the insight cleanly.
Claude.topIssue: No recurring named character carries the arc across lessons — the module leans on rotating case studies as its 'characters,' which is defensible at Advanced/technical register but weakens Character Consistency (D1 c4) against the rubric.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of agent, ReAct, tool use, Goodhart, least privilege, blast radius, and direct/indirect injection are precise and consistent with Anthropic/DeepMind/OWASP framings; quizzes actively defuse the standard misconceptions (agent = smarter chatbot, prompt injection = jailbreak, longer prompt = safer).
Gemini.topIssue: Several case citations are stated with specificity that outruns the public record — the 'University of Wisconsin' 2023 exfiltration demo, the 'Delphina' 100%-coverage case study, and the venue/month for Michael Bargury's Copilot demo are the ones most likely to fail a fact-check and should be re-sourced.

Perplexity.notes: The example set — Devin, Cursor billing, Operator, Claude computer use, Agentforce, Copilot Studio, OWASP LLM Top 10, Rehberger, Bargury, CMU image-injection — is exactly the last-12-month surface a learner will meet in the wild, and the labs push directly into the judgment work a practitioner does today.
Perplexity.topIssue: Lab executability depends on a live tutor endpoint (/aesop-api/proxy.php) — the pedagogy is strong but the applied experience degrades to a static prompt list wherever that backend is not reachable, so the D5 c1 ceiling is only as high as deployment reliability.

modules.module: M2: Failure Modes: How Agents Go Off the Rails

Claude.notes: Strong technical narrative structure with documented cases opening each lesson, but story-scenes are brief single paragraphs that push narrative density below the 20-35% Advanced target.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative density runs closer to 10-15% — each lesson leans heavily on expository concept sections after a one-paragraph story opener, missing the storytelling weight Advanced learners can absorb.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of specification gaming, reward hacking, indirect prompt injection, deceptive alignment and instrumental convergence are textbook-precise and case citations (CoastRunners, Air Canada BC CRT, Sleeper Agents, Apollo, OWASP) are largely accurate with correct dates and actors.
Gemini.topIssue: Instrumental convergence is attributed to Bostrom and Russell but omits Steve Omohundro's earlier 'Basic AI Drives' framing; the Frances Haugen framing also compresses her testimony into a specification-gaming interpretation that is defensible but not verbatim.

Perplexity.notes: Cases through Dec 2024 (Apollo, Sleeper Agents, Air Canada) are current and representative, and labs map to real 2024-era deployment scenarios (customer support agent, email-reading agent, alignment evaluator).
Perplexity.topIssue: Content stops at December 2024 with no 2025 developments (o1/o3 scheming follow-ups, Anthropic's alignment audits, evolving prompt-injection defenses) — 20 months stale for a module framed around 'currently deployed' agents in mid-2026.

Claude.notes: Strong narrative-analytical rhythm: each lesson opens with a dated story-scene (2010 Flash Crash, Moffatt v. Air Canada, ProPublica/COMPAS, Herzberg/Tempe) before pivoting to systemic analysis, and the 'objective specification failure' thread is threaded consistently through all four lessons — good curricular closure.
Claude.topIssue: Instagram statistic is internally inconsistent: prose says 'roughly 13.5% of teenage girls' and then quotes an internal Facebook memo 'one in three teen girls' as if these are the same figure — the Q4-3 feedback compounds this by conflating '13.5%' with 'roughly one in three'.

Gemini.notes: Definitional work is precise — algorithmic fairness impossibility, proxy discrimination, prompt injection with the SQL-injection analogy — and the Northpointe-vs-ProPublica framing is handled honestly, but at least one datapoint conflict and several near-misses accumulate around Instagram figures, dates, and 'first' attributions.
Gemini.topIssue: Instagram statistic contradiction: '13.5% of teenage girls' cannot be reconciled with the quoted internal memo phrase 'one in three teen girls' — the Q4-3 feedback explicitly claims '13.5% — roughly one in three,' which is a factual/arithmetic error a technical reviewer will flag immediately.

Perplexity.notes: Incidents cited are real, cite-able, and consequential — Moffatt v. Air Canada, SEC/CFTC 2010 report, ProPublica investigation, Obermeyer et al. Science 2019, NTSB HAR-19/03, Haugen disclosures — but the sample stops mid-2024 with nothing from the last 12–18 months of agent deployments.
Perplexity.topIssue: Recency gap: for an Advanced 2026 module, the sample stops mid-2024 and does not reflect the last 12–18 months of agent deployments (computer-use agents, MCP ecosystem, 2025 prompt-injection disclosures, EU AI Act operational phase). Cases are canonical but the module reads more like a 2024 retrospective than a current-events unit.

modules.module: M4: The Control Problem — AI Agent Safety

Claude.notes: Story-scenes are precise, well-labeled documented incidents (GPT-4 shutdown, USAF drone, Sydney, Anthropic Constitutional AI) that anchor each lesson with real stakes; voice is technical and journalistically consistent, though narrative density feels closer to 15-18% than the 20-35% target.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative density sits below the 20-35% target; story-scenes are opening hooks rather than sustained narrative — no character or arc carries between lessons.

Gemini.notes: Instrumental convergence, corrigibility (correctly attributed to Armstrong/Soares/Fallenstein 2015 MIRI), HITL/HOTL, defense-in-depth, and scalable oversight are framed consistent with published literature, though a few incident framings and citations (GPT-4 'preserved operational state', Apollo 2023 backup-actions paper) are more definitive than the underlying evidence supports.
Gemini.topIssue: A few incident framings ('preserved its operational state', Apollo 2023 backup-actions paper) are more definitive than the underlying evidence supports and would benefit from either softening or more precise citation.

Perplexity.notes: Remarkably current: OpenAI preparedness framework, Anthropic 2024 model card, UK AISI evaluations, NIST AI RMF, DeepMind 2024 safety spec, Alignment Faking paper — and lab scenarios (contract-management agent, ICU sepsis, fintech portfolio manager, pharma FDA submissions) are realistic deployment shapes practitioners actually face today.
Perplexity.topIssue: Register and lab scenarios (fintech, FDA submissions, ICU) target the upper end of the age range — a 13-14-year-old will find the business framing distant even if the concepts are reachable.

modules.module: M5: Evaluating an Agent Before You Trust It With Anything

Claude.notes: Strong curriculum arc: each lesson opens with one real-event story-scene (Amazon, Sydney, Chevrolet, Knight Capital) then unfolds a matching evaluation dimension, with a 'Module 5 Frame' gold callout that sets the four-part promise and gets delivered on end-to-end.
Claude.topIssue: L1 introduces a numbered 'Three Dimensions' heading but immediately shows four cards (Task Fidelity, Goal Alignment, Boundary Respect, Failure Transparency) — small counting mismatch reader will notice.

Gemini.notes: Core facts hold — Amazon Reuters disclosure (2018), Roose/von Hagen Sydney incidents (Feb 2023), Knight Capital $440M/45min (Aug 2012), Moffatt v. Air Canada (Feb 2024), Chris Bakke's Watsonville Chevrolet $1 Tahoe, DeepMind Sparrow, Anthropic sycophancy research — with technical vocabulary used precisely.
Gemini.topIssue: Two loose citations weaken sourcing rigor: (1) 'Stanford and UC Berkeley March 2023' research on GPT-4 browser agents is not tied to a specific paper (reads like a paraphrase of several results) and (2) the Constitutional AI paper (Bai et al. 2022) does not explicitly document 'deliberate failure mode injection' by that name.

Perplexity.notes: Currency is a standout: every real-world anchor is from the actual pre-deployment-evaluation news cycle (2012 Knight; 2018 Amazon; 2022 Sparrow; Feb 2023 Sydney; Dec 2023 Chevrolet; Feb 2024 Air Canada; 2023 SEC surveillance actions), and the Air Canada + Knight Capital Principle callouts are exactly the takeaways a practitioner would want internalized before wiring an agent to production.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 2023 SEC enforcement reference generalizes 'multiple broker-dealer firms' without naming any (e.g., no reference to specific settlements). For an Advanced learner, one named enforcement action would harden the claim.

modules.module: M6: Safety Red Flags Every User Should Know

Claude.notes: Four discrete case-study anchors (Air Canada, Sydney/Goodside, Mata v. Avianca, AF447) function as strong per-lesson openers rather than a serialized through-line — acceptable for advanced/technical register but leaves narrative density on the low edge of the 20–35% band.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative density skews low; each lesson uses a single one-paragraph vignette, so the 'story-driven' framing is thinner than the curriculum baseline expects even for advanced level.

Gemini.notes: Core failure taxonomies (scope violation, indirect prompt injection, hallucinated tool calls, automation bias) are technically sound, and the compound-probability example in Q3-2 (1−0.85^5 ≈ 56%) is mathematically correct, but several attributions are difficult to verify — 'Microsoft researcher Kalinda Martin' has no verifiable footprint, and Robert Williams's wrongful arrest is widely documented as DataWorks Plus (NEC/Rank One), not Amazon Rekognition.
Gemini.topIssue: The Robert Williams / Amazon Rekognition attribution is a substantive factual error repeated in both the lesson prose and the module test key; needs correction to the actual DataWorks Plus / Michigan State Police face-match pipeline.

Perplexity.notes: Case selection is unusually current and well-chosen for the theme (Moffatt v. Air Canada Feb 2024, Goodside Sept 2022, Sydney Feb 2023, Mata v. Avianca June 2023 with the verified $5,000 fine, Rehberger indirect-injection work, AF447/BEA 2012, NIST FRVT Part 3), and lab scenarios reflect real deployed patterns.
Perplexity.topIssue: Currency of statistics — several 2023-vintage numbers (60% injection success, 19.7% package hallucination, 15–30% tool-call hallucination) are presented without model-version pinning and are almost certainly not representative of frontier-model behavior in 2026.

modules.module: M7: AI Agents: Who's Responsible When an Agent Messes Up?

Claude.notes: Well-structured Advanced module with strong applied labs and a clean lesson-quiz-lab-test scaffold; story-scenes (Flash Crash, Watson, Uber, EU AI Act) open each lesson vividly but occupy only ~10-15% of content, below the 20-35% narrative density expected for the tier.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative density is thin for the Advanced tier: real-event scenes are one paragraph each and act as hooks rather than sustained story, leaving the module reading more like a legal white paper than a story-driven lesson.

Gemini.notes: Historical incidents are cited with reasonable fidelity (Flash Crash/Sarao, Tay's 16-hour lifespan, Watson for Oncology, Uber Tempe with disabled emergency braking, Schwartz/LoDuca sanctions, Amazon hiring tool) and legal frameworks (NIST AI RMF Govern-Map-Measure-Manage, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certifiability, NYC Local Law 144, EU AI Act €35M/7% penalties) are accurate.
Gemini.topIssue: A couple of attributions are slightly imprecise (Gebru firing dated 2021 vs. Dec 2020; 'accountability gap' attributed too specifically to Pasquale), and the density of legal terminology pushes cognitive load above the 13-year-old end of the target range.

Perplexity.notes: Currency is a standout — EU AI Act entry into force August 1, 2024 with correct staged timeline, correct maximum penalty (€35M/7% turnover), correct classification of credit-scoring and hiring as high-risk, accurate NIST AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023) with Govern-Map-Measure-Manage functions, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 as first certifiable AIMS, NYC Local Law 144, and Biden's October 2023 EO all cleanly presented.
Perplexity.topIssue: AI Liability Directive discussion doesn't flag that the Commission withdrew the draft in Feb 2025, so learners may believe the presumption-of-fault mechanism is still an active EU proposal rather than a case study of a shelved reform.

modules.module: M8: Applying a Safety Lens to Your Own AI Use

Claude.notes: Strong capstone architecture: each lesson opens on a documented incident (Samsung, Air Canada, Rite Aid, Stanford Copilot) and closes on a synthesized 90-day plan lab; the audit→habits→communication→sustainability arc is genuinely coherent and explicitly calls back to every prior incident in the course.
Claude.topIssue: The 'four audit dimensions' framework is attributed to unnamed 'researchers and practitioners' — feels synthesized-for-curriculum rather than sourced, which is a minor integrity gap in an otherwise well-cited module.

Gemini.notes: Most citations check out (Samsung April 2023 three incidents in ~20 days, Moffatt v. Air Canada BCCRT Feb 2024, Mata v. Avianca / Schwartz six fabricated citations, FTC Rite Aid Dec 2023 five-year ban, STAT News 2018 Watson phrasing, Bainbridge 1983 Automatica, Gollwitzer implementation intentions, Perry et al. Stanford Copilot 2022), but 'confidence inversion' is used as a defined term when the actual literature is automation bias/complacency.
Gemini.topIssue: 'Confidence inversion' presented as if it were an established research term when the actual literature term is automation bias/complacency; the framework's academic attribution is vague.

Perplexity.notes: Currency is a genuine strength — 2023-2024 incidents (Samsung April 2023, Moffatt Feb 2024, FTC Rite Aid Dec 2023, Mata v. Avianca May 2023) alongside canonical older references (Bainbridge 1983, Edmondson psychological safety, Gollwitzer) — and the three-tier sustainability system points learners at NIST AI RMF and the AI Incident Database, the actually-authoritative sources practitioners use in 2025-2026.
Perplexity.topIssue: Minor: the 'authoritative sources' list could name specific practitioner newsletters rather than leave that as a placeholder — but the framework for choosing them is sound.
